opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we think about a lot, because the answer keeps changing as the models get better.

In the early days, the center of gravity was almost entirely on the machine learning side. We needed people who could build and train really large models, who understood the architectures and the data pipelines and how to make them work at scale. That's still at the core of what we do. But as the models have gotten more capable, the bottleneck has shifted. It's less "can we predict this structure or design this molecule at all?" and more "is this the right molecule to make, and does it actually behave the way we need it to in the real world?"

So the mix has gradually tilted toward people with deep drug discovery intuition: medicinal chemists, protein engineers, biologists who've spent years watching programs succeed and fail. They know which properties really matter, what a good starting point looks like, and where the models might be fooling you. That kind of judgment is very hard to replace, and it becomes more valuable as the models produce more candidates, because someone has to decide what's worth pursuing.

What I've found most important is that we don't keep those groups in separate silos. The best work happens when an ML researcher and a chemist sit together and argue about why a design looks wrong, or why the model is confident about something a scientist doesn't trust. That back-and-forth shapes what we train on, how we evaluate, and ultimately what we build. So I'd say we want people who are excellent at one thing and genuinely curious about the other side. That bilingual quality has become one of the main things we hire for.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's shifted a lot in a pretty short time. When we started Chai, the team was heavily weighted toward machine learning — people who had built large models before and knew how to make them train well. The biology side was important, but it was more like the problem definition. We needed enough domain depth to know what a good structure prediction looked like, what the benchmarks were, where the data was flawed.

What's changed as the models have gotten better is that the limiting factor stops being "can we get the model to work" and becomes "do we actually know what the right question is." So now we have way more people with wet-lab backgrounds, people who've run antibody campaigns, people who've been through the pain of taking a design from a computer into a cell and watching it fail for reasons that had nothing to do with binding affinity. That experience is really hard to fake, and it's the thing that tells us which of the model's outputs are actually useful and which are just technically impressive.

The other piece is that the two groups can't be siloed. The version that doesn't work is where the biologists hand requirements to the ML people and wait. The version that works is where a biologist sits with the person training the model and says, "this prediction is confidently wrong, and here's the physical reason why," and that feeds directly into how we build the next version. So we look for people on both sides who are curious enough about the other discipline to have that conversation. You don't need to be a dual expert, but you need to be able to hold both in your head a little bit.

And as the models keep improving, I think the mix keeps tilting toward people who can design and run experiments, because the models will generate hypotheses faster than anyone can test them. The bottleneck becomes validation.

astra-6.text:
I think the mix evolves as the models improve. You need people who can push the machine learning forward, but you also need people who understand biology and can ask whether an improvement in the model actually translates into a better molecule or a more useful experiment.

Those aren’t separate problems. The experiments you choose determine what you learn, and what you learn should inform the next model. So the important thing is having people who can work across those boundaries—a machine learning researcher who wants to understand why an experiment failed, and a biologist who wants to understand what the model is capturing.

As the models become more capable, that scientific judgment becomes even more valuable. You have more things you could try, so deciding what’s worth trying becomes a bigger part of the work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the mix changes as the models get better. Early on, a lot of the work is about getting the machine learning to work: the architecture, the data, the training. As the models become more capable, the question increasingly becomes, what should we ask them to do, and how do we know whether the answer is useful? That takes deep expertise in biology, chemistry, and experimental work.

So I don’t think better models make domain expertise less important. They make it more valuable, because you can explore more possibilities, and you need good judgment about which ones matter. The team we want is one where those disciplines work closely together—where an experimental result can inform the next model, and a model’s capabilities can change how you design the next experiment.
